headline.statement: Ten of the 27 FIM means in Table IV cannot be the average of any set of whole-number scores from the group sizes the paper states, and all ten fall in the two comparison groups while the Cerebrolysin group's nine means all check out.
headline.evidence: Group II (n = 18): "the FIM score increased from 88.23 to 98.24 at 6 months (p = 0.55) and to 104.88 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.23 to 66.52 at 6 months (p = 0.079)". Group III (n = 30): "In the BFT group the FIM score increased from 88.28 to 96.95 at 6 months (p = 0.005), and to 100.85 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.06 to 65.17 at 6 months (p = 0.040) and at 12 months to 67.68 (p = 0.001), while the cognition score increased from 29.22 to 31.78 at 6 months (p = 0.159)". For n = 30 a mean must be a whole number divided by 30: the nearest reachable values to 88.28 are 88.27 and 88.30; to 96.95 they are 96.93 and 96.97; to 100.85 they are 100.83 and 100.87. Every one of these ten values is printed twice in the article, once in Table IV and once in the Results prose.
headline.plain: The paper reports average disability scores for three groups of patients. Those scores are whole numbers for each patient, so any group average has to be a whole number divided by the number of patients in that group. Ten of the reported averages are not -- there is no combination of patient scores in a group of 18 or 30 that would produce them. All ten belong to the two groups the treatment was compared against; the treatment group's own figures are all reachable.

findings.title: Ten Table IV FIM means unreachable from any sample of the stated group size
findings.location: Table IV (Evolution of the FIM score), Motor / Cognition / Total rows for BFT + Lokomat (n = 18) and BFT (n = 30); the same ten values also appear in Results, FIM Scale, paras 3-4
findings.reported: Table IV prints 27 mean +/- dispersion cells across three groups. For n = 18: 59.23, 66.52, 88.23, 98.24. For n = 30: 29.22, 31.78, 67.68, 88.28, 96.95, 100.85.
findings.computed: All ten fail GRIM with failure_mode 'granularity'. Re-run in this stage on the six n = 30 cells via check_table: 18 of 18 checks returned impossible, 0 refused (GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE each). Example: for n = 30 the nearest integer sum to 88.28 is 2648, giving 88.266667, which does not round back to 88.28. R `scrutiny` was run independently on 59.23/n=18, 88.28/n=30 and 100.85/n=30 and returned inconsistent for all three; the sweep had separately confirmed 59.23/18, 88.23/18, 29.22/30 and 96.95/30 against the same engine. Both engines agree on every value cross-checked. The corresponding nine means for the Cerebrolysin group (n = 22) all pass.
findings.assumptions: GRIM here requires only that each patient's FIM score is a whole number and that the mean was taken over the group size printed in the table header. The paper states FIM items are scored on 'a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 (totally independent) to 1 (totally dependent)', so the summed scores are integers; the group sizes n = 22 / 18 / 30 are stated in the table headers and in the Study design. The failure mode returned is granularity, which does NOT depend on the assumed 13-91 / 5-35 / 18-126 scale limits, so rulebook rule 4's cap does not apply. The single benign explanation that would dissolve this finding is per-timepoint missing data making the true denominator smaller than the printed n -- but the paper reports no attrition and states the analytic sample had complete datasets. Extraction error is effectively excluded: the sweep reconciled Table IV against the PDF version of record cell by cell, all ten values are printed a second time in the Results prose, and this stage re-pulled the table independently.

consequence.explanation: Table IV is the only source in the paper for every FIM figure, so the nine reported FIM ANOVAs and the stated conclusion that 'the best ES was recorded for the group combining all three associated therapies' rest on numbers that cannot have come from the samples described.

findings.plain: Each patient's functional-independence score is a whole number, so a group average has to be that group's total divided by the number of patients -- for 30 patients, only certain two-decimal values are possible. Ten reported averages are not among them, meaning no group of the stated size could have produced them. Two independent statistical packages agree. All ten belong to the two groups used for comparison; the group that received the drug has no such problem, which is the reverse of what a simple typesetting accident would look like.

findings.title: Every ANOVA F statistic tested irreconcilable with the means and standard deviations printed beside it
findings.location: Results: Barthel Index para 1, FIM Scale para 1, SS-QOL Scale para 1; inputs from Tables II, IV and V
findings.reported: 24 F statistics, none with degrees of freedom. Barthel Group I: 'F = 4.766, p = 0.012'. Barthel control: 'F = 3.122, p = 0.049'. SS-QOL total Group I: 'F = 21.217, p < 0.001'.
findings.computed: Three F values re-tested in this stage, all outside the interval reachable from the paper's own printed means and SDs, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of 0 over 5,000 draws of the rounding box. Barthel Group I (means 51.14/59.77/65.91, SDs 9.36/10.22/10.82, n = 22 each): achievable F [11.732, 11.783], reported 4.766; achievable p [4.50e-05, 4.67e-05], reported 0.012. Barthel control (means 50.50/55.67/58.83, SDs 10.14/11.11/11.74, n = 30 each): achievable F [4.359, 4.387], reported 3.122; achievable p [0.0153, 0.0157], reported 0.049. SS-QOL total Group I (means 146.14/164.73/179.14, SDs 17.69/18.32/18.64, n = 22 each): achievable F [18.120, 18.158], reported 21.217. The sweep tested five and all five failed.
findings.assumptions: The recomputation treats each within-group time effect as the one-way ANOVA over three timepoints that the paper says it ran, and treats the tabulated dispersions as SDs. Two alternative readings were considered and neither rescues the pattern: a repeated-measures analysis removes between-subject error and would RAISE F, but four of the five misses are in the direction of the reported F being too SMALL; reading the dispersion as the SEM that Table II's row label states would LOWER F drastically (roughly 0.5 for Barthel Group I), but one miss is in the direction of the reported F being too LARGE. No single explanation covers both directions. For three of the FIM recomputations the input means are themselves among the ten GRIM failures above, so those inputs are already in question.

consequence.explanation: The 24 F statistics are the paper's entire evidence that 'Evolution of the functional independence was statistically significant for all studied groups' and that quality of life improved significantly in all three arms; whether any of them crosses the paper's alpha cannot be settled, because under the SD reading the true p-values are smaller than printed and under the SEM reading several would become non-significant.

findings.plain: For each outcome the paper reports a test statistic summarising how much scores changed over 12 months. That statistic can be recalculated from the averages and spreads printed in the same tables. Every one recalculated -- five by the initial sweep, three re-checked here -- comes out to a different number than the paper reports, and the mismatches go in both directions, so no single mistake such as using the wrong kind of test explains them. Because the paper never states how many patients and groups fed each test, there is no other way to check them.

findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.reported: "the percentage of patients with a score >= 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016)"
findings.computed: Re-run in this stage: 13.04% of n = 22 implies 2.8688 patients. The reachable values around it are 9.09 (2/22), 13.64 (3/22) and 18.18 (4/22). Separately, the two components sum to 31.22, not the stated 31.82, a gap of 0.60 against a rounding tolerance of 0.015. findings.assumptions: Requires only that a count of patients out of the stated 22 is a whole number; n = 22 is stated in the Study design and in every table header. consequence.explanation: Affects the arithmetic of one descriptive sentence only; the direction and reported significance of the Group I spasticity change rest on Table III's counts and on p = 0.016, neither of which depends on this decomposition.

findings.plain: The paper says the share of patients with high muscle stiffness fell by 18.18% and then a further 13.04%, totalling 31.82%. With 22 patients, a percentage has to be a whole number of patients out of 22, and 13.04% is not -- it works out to 2.87 people. It is also 0.6 short of adding up to the stated total. Using 13.64% instead, which is exactly 3 of 22, makes both problems vanish and matches the counts in the paper's own table, so this looks like a typing slip rather than anything more. It changes nothing else in the paper.

findings.title: Bonferroni correction claimed in the Methods but reported p-values match uncorrected tests
findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results, SS-QOL Scale, final paragraph; means and SDs from Table V
findings.reported: Methods: "ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups". Results: SS-QOL total higher in Group I than control at 12 months, p = 0.040; mental score p = 0.024 at 6 months and p = 0.002 at 12 months.
findings.computed: The sweep recomputed both from Table V as ordinary two-sample t-tests. SS-QOL total (179.14 +/- 18.64, n = 22 vs 168.77 +/- 16.44, n = 30): Welch p = 0.0435, Student p = 0.0387 against a reported 0.040. SS-QOL mental (32.27 +/- 4.28, n = 22 vs 28.17 +/- 3.11, n = 30): Welch p = 0.00051, Student p = 0.00021 against a reported 0.002. The reported values track the uncorrected comparison. multiplicity_report was run four times across the two stages -- three by the sweep, once here with the correction field omitted -- and returned n_tests = 0 every time, so the number of claims that would not survive correction could not be computed.
findings.assumptions: That the three group contrasts (I vs III, II vs III, I vs II) form one family per outcome, which is what the Methods' own reference to a Bonferroni post-hoc implies. I did not compute an adjusted threshold by hand; the tool that does that arithmetic refused, and this finding rests only on the tool-computed observation that the printed p-values match the uncorrected tests.

consequence.explanation: The paper's only direct between-group superiority claims -- that quality of life was better in the Cerebrolysin arm than in the control arm at 6 and 12 months -- are the ones closest to the 0.05 threshold, and whether they survive the correction the Methods claim was applied could not be determined because the multiplicity tool would not run.

findings.plain: When several comparisons are made on the same patients, the usual safeguard is to demand stronger evidence from each one, and the paper says it used such a safeguard. But the reported significance values match what you get without it. The paper's central claim -- that the drug group did better than the control group on quality of life -- is reported at a value just inside the usual cutoff, so it is exactly the kind of result the safeguard exists to catch. We could not compute how many of these claims would survive, because the tool for that arithmetic would not run on this input.

findings.title: Statement that no baseline characteristic differed contradicted by the sex split in Table I
findings.location: Table I, Gender rows; claim in Results, Patient characteristics, and in Study design
findings.reported: "In terms of demographic and clinical characteristics, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups (Table I )." Table I: Females 3 (13.64%), 3 (16.67%), 14 (46.67%); Males 19 (86.36%), 15 (83.33%), 16 (53.33%).
findings.computed: Re-run in this stage on the counts re-read from Table I: chi-squared = 8.4679, df = 2, p = 0.0145. Expected female counts under no difference would be 6.29, 5.14 and 8.57 against observed 3, 3 and 14.
findings.assumptions: Table I prints no per-row p-values, so this is a recomputation against a blanket claim rather than a disagreement with a stated statistic. Note that allocation here was explicitly NOT random -- 'Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat' -- so an imbalance is expected. What is flagged is the claim that none exists, not the imbalance itself. For the same reason the baseline-uniformity tests (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion) were deliberately not run: they ask whether groups are MORE alike than random allocation permits, and that null does not apply to a non-randomised study.

consequence.explanation: Every between-group comparison in the paper assumes the arms were comparable, and no outcome analysis adjusts for sex, so a control arm that is 47% female against 14% and 17% in the treated arms is an uncontrolled difference the paper states does not exist.

findings.plain: The paper says the three groups were alike at the start. They were not alike in one respect that it prints itself: the comparison group was about 47% women, the two treated groups about 14% and 17%. A difference that large would not usually arise by chance. Patients were not assigned to groups at random -- they were placed by their medical history and willingness to use the robot -- so an imbalance is unsurprising; the problem is the flat statement that there was none, combined with the fact that no later analysis adjusts for it.

findings.title: Dispersion labelled SEM in Table II, unlabelled in Tables IV and V, and used as a standard deviation
findings.location: Table II row label 'Mean +/- SEM'; Tables IV and V, all '+/-' cells; Methods, effect-size definition
findings.reported: Table II: "Mean +/- SEM  51.14 +/- 9.36". Methods: "ES = m1 - m2/s1, where ... s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score." Tables IV and V print '+/-' with no SD or SEM designation in caption, header or footnote.
findings.computed: Taken as an SD, 9.36 at n = 22 implies a standard error of 2.00 and sits at 18% of the ceiling for a 0-100 instrument. Taken as the SEM the label states, it implies an SD of 43.9, which is 86% of that ceiling. The tool's likely interpretation is SD. The effect sizes printed in Table II are reproduced by dividing the mean change by the tabulated dispersion, which is what the paper's own formula does with an SD.
findings.assumptions: The 0-100 Barthel range used for the plausibility ceiling is MY assumption, not the paper's -- the paper describes the instrument only as testing '10 stages for using the 10 ADL for self-care'. Per rulebook rule 4 this caps the severity at suspicious and disqualifies it as a headline. The likeliest explanation is simple mislabelling of the row: Olsen (2002) found 40% of studies reporting 'SD' had reported the standard error, and the same confusion in reverse is entirely ordinary. But the paper never resolves it, and the consequence is not cosmetic.

consequence.explanation: All 52 effect sizes in Tables II, IV and V, and every ANOVA recomputation, depend on whether the printed '+/-' value is a standard deviation or a standard error; under the SEM reading the paper's effect sizes would be roughly 4.7 times smaller, turning the 'large' effects its conclusions rest on into small ones.

findings.plain: The tables print a number after each average that describes how spread out the patients were. One table labels it as one kind of spread measure, the other two label it as nothing at all, and the paper's own effect-size formula treats it as a third thing. These differ by a factor of about five at these sample sizes. If the label on the first table is taken at face value, the paper's headline finding of large treatment effects becomes a finding of small ones. The most likely explanation is a mislabelled row -- a very common slip -- but as printed the reader cannot tell which reading is intended.

findings.title: Three measurements on the same patients analysed as a one-way ANOVA across independent groups
findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results, all within-group time effects
findings.reported: "ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups for evaluations, where the compared data were expressed as an average", and every within-group time effect is described as 'one-way ANOVA' over baseline, 6 months and 12 months.
findings.computed: No arithmetic tool applies. Baseline, 6-month and 12-month scores are three measurements on the SAME 22 / 18 / 30 patients, which violates the independence assumption a one-way ANOVA requires; a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model is the matching analysis. Direction of the resulting bias: treating correlated measurements as independent inflates the error term and makes the test conservative, so this does not on its own explain the F discrepancies in finding 2, four of five of which run the other way.
findings.assumptions: Rulebook rule 5 (design validity). This is a reading of the Methods, not a recomputation, and the severity reflects that. Related reporting gaps recorded here rather than as separate findings: allocation was explicitly non-random, there is no trial registration number, no CONSORT flow diagram, and no adverse-event reporting for a 12-month intravenous drug protocol.

consequence.explanation: All 24 within-group time effects -- the paper's evidence that each therapy produced significant improvement -- use a test that does not match the repeated-measures structure of the data.

findings.plain: The same patients were measured three times, at the start, at six months and at a year. The paper analyses those three sets of measurements as though they came from three different groups of people, which is not the right test for repeated measurements on the same individuals. The correct test would normally make the results look stronger, not weaker, so this is a methodological mismatch rather than an explanation of the other problems -- but it means the reported comparisons were not computed the way the design required.

findings.title: Sample-size formula containing no power term presented as delivering 80% power
findings.reported: "A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at alpha = 0.05 and a test power at 1-beta = 0.80 ... n = N * X / X + N - 1 ... where X = Z^2 alpha/2 * p * (1-p) / MOE^2 ... According to this formula, the sample size should be higher or equal to 70."
findings.computed: verify_power_analysis returned indeterminate: the calculation cannot be reproduced because no effect size is stated. Beyond that, the formula the paper prints is the standard expression for estimating a PROPORTION in a finite population to a given margin of error. It contains no beta and no power term, so it cannot yield '1-beta = 0.80', and the paper states neither the proportion p, nor the margin of error MOE, nor the population size N that the formula requires.
findings.assumptions: The observation that the printed formula contains no power term is a reading of the Methods text, not a tool result; the tool result behind this finding is only the indeterminate verdict from the missing effect size. Also worth a reader's attention without any inference drawn: the required N derived from this formula (>= 70) exactly equals the number recruited (70).

consequence.explanation: No specific result depends on this, but the adequacy of the sample size cannot be assessed from anything the paper reports.

findings.plain: The paper says it worked out how many patients it needed to have an 80% chance of detecting a real effect. The formula it prints does something different -- it estimates how many people you need to measure a percentage to within a given margin of error -- and contains nothing corresponding to that 80%. It also leaves out three of the quantities the formula needs. So the stated justification for the sample size cannot be reproduced or checked.

findings.title: Between-group quality-of-life effect at or above the 95th percentile for clinical medicine
findings.location: Table V, Mental rows at 12 months, Group I versus Group III
findings.reported: Mental domain at 12 months: 32.27 +/- 4.28 (n = 22) in the Cerebrolysin arm against 28.17 +/- 3.11 (n = 30) in the control arm. The paper's own within-group effect size for that cell is 2.11.
findings.computed: Cohen's d = 1.12, Hedges' g = 1.11 on a pooled SD of 3.65 with df = 50 -- at or above the 95th percentile of the tool's benchmark distribution for clinical medicine.
findings.assumptions: The benchmark percentiles the tool used (median 0.30, 75th 0.55, 95th 1.00) are flagged in its own output as an uncited estimate rather than a published table, so this is a soft comparison. Two of the three ordinary causes of an inflated effect cannot be excluded: the SD/SEM ambiguity in finding 6 (which would move the effect the other way) and the fact that the SS-QOL scoring range is never stated, so a scale mismatch cannot be ruled out. The third is ruled out -- the comparator is active (balneo-physiotherapy), not a waiting list. Severity is capped at suspicious; a large effect is unusual, never impossible.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the plausibility of the paper's central claim that adding Cerebrolysin to robotic gait training and physiotherapy produces a large quality-of-life advantage over physiotherapy alone.

findings.plain: The reported advantage of the drug group over the comparison group on the mental quality-of-life measure is larger than roughly 95% of effects reported in clinical medicine, from an add-on treatment tested against an active alternative rather than against nothing. That is not impossible and is not evidence of any error by itself, but it is unusual enough to warrant seeing the underlying data. The comparison benchmark used here is an estimate rather than a published reference table, so treat this as a soft signal.

findings.title: Degrees of freedom absent from all 24 reported F tests
findings.reported: "total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group" -- the form used for all 24 F statistics.
findings.computed: statcheck extracted zero test statistics from the complete Results text. This is not a tool failure: every F is printed without degrees of freedom, and without them an F cannot be converted to a p-value, so no automated consistency check is possible. Verification of the F statistics therefore had to proceed indirectly, by recomputation from the group means and SDs (finding 2).
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own text. This is a refusal to judge, not a defect claim in itself -- but the omission is what forces every check of the paper's inferential statistics through the tables.
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group"

consequence.explanation: None of the 24 reported F tests can be checked by the standard automated route, so all verification of them depends on recomputation from tables whose own values are partly in question.

findings.plain: Whenever a paper reports this kind of test it should also report how many groups and how many patients went into it. This paper never does, in any of its 24 tests. Without those figures the reported result cannot be checked against the reported significance value by any standard method, and the only route left is to rebuild the test from the tables -- which is what was done, and which is where the mismatches in the second finding come from.

findings.title: Figure 1 caption grading p = 0.057 as 'weakly significant' against the paper's stated threshold of 0.05
findings.reported: Methods: "Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05." Fig. 1 caption: "illustrates a highly statistically significant decrease (p=0.016) for the BFT+Lokomat+Cerebrolysin group, weakly significant (p=0.057) for the BFT+Lokomat group and not significant (p=0.595) for the BFT group."

findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The figure carries no values that are not already printed in Table III and the Results text, so nothing was lost by not reading the plotted bars.

consequence.explanation: Applying the paper's own stated threshold of p < 0.05 makes the Group II spasticity reduction non-significant, where the caption presents it as partially supporting the conclusion that Lokomat therapy reduces spasticity.

findings.plain: The paper states up front that it will call a result significant when its significance value is below 0.05. The figure caption then describes a value of 0.057 as 'weakly significant'. By the paper's own rule that result is simply not significant, so a null finding is being presented as partial support for the conclusion.

Both tests ask whether groups are MORE similar than random allocation allows; allocation here was explicitly non-random ('Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat'). Their null does not apply and running them would have manufactured a verdict.

limitations: FIGURES: this agent reads text and tables. No figure image was rendered or read in either stage of this review. The paper contains one figure, and its caption was read as text from page 6 of the PDF; the sweep recorded that Fig. 1 carries no values that are not already printed in Table III and the Results text, so no unique data were lost. Nothing in this report rests on reading a plotted mark.

Two of the four questions Heathers says a granularity or similarity result must be read against are outside this system's reach entirely: it reads one paper and reaches no network, so it cannot tell you whether similar patterns appear in other papers by these authors (the article itself cites Uivarosan et al., 2018 on the same topic), nor what the equivalent recomputed values look like in comparable stroke-rehabilitation trials. The interpretation of the Table IV granularity finding is therefore partly ours and partly the reader's.

The multiplicity arithmetic could not be obtained. multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 on four separate attempts across both stages, so no count of claims lost to correction backs finding 4; only the tool-computed observation that the reported p-values match uncorrected tests does. No hand-computed substitute was used.

A direct re-run of grim_check on individual Table IV means failed with a parameter-type error in the tool's decimals handling. Our engine's verdict was obtained instead through check_table, which routes the same GRIM implementation and returned impossible on 18 of 18 checks for the n = 30 block. This is a limitation of one calling path, not of the result, and R scrutiny was run independently on three of the same values.

The Barthel range of 0-100 used for the SD-versus-SEM plausibility ceiling, and the SS-QOL domain range of 0-245, are assumptions this reviewer supplied; the paper states neither. Both findings that depend on them are capped at suspicious and name the assumption, and neither is the headline.
Sixteen of the paper's 24 F statistics were not individually recomputed. The eight that were all failed, but the generalisation to the remainder is an extrapolation.

No raw or participant-level data accompany the article, so the duplication and reconstruction checks that work on raw data could not be attempted; the duplication analysis reported here operated on summary statistics only.

questions_for_authors.question: Table IV reports FIM means of 88.28, 96.95 and 100.85 for the BFT group (n = 30) and 59.23, 66.52, 88.23 and 98.24 for the BFT + Lokomat group (n = 18). Because FIM scores are sums of whole-number item ratings, a mean over 30 patients must be a whole number divided by 30 -- the nearest reachable values to 88.28 are 88.27 and 88.30 -- and none of these ten values is reachable at the stated group size, while all nine means for the n = 22 group are. Could you confirm the number of patients contributing to each FIM cell at each timepoint, and say whether any FIM scores were prorated or imputed?
questions_for_authors.why: Directly tests the only benign explanation for the headline finding: that the effective denominator differs from the printed group size because of missing data at a timepoint.

questions_for_authors.question: The paper reports 24 F statistics without degrees of freedom. Recomputing three of them as the one-way ANOVAs the Results describe, from the means and SDs printed in the same tables, gives F between 11.73 and 11.78 for the Barthel Group I comparison against a reported 4.766; F between 4.36 and 4.39 for the Barthel control group against a reported 3.122; and F between 18.12 and 18.16 for the SS-QOL total in Group I against a reported 21.217. Could you supply the degrees of freedom and the SPSS output for these three tests?
questions_for_authors.why: The misses run in both directions, which excludes the tidy explanations (repeated-measures analysis, or SEM read as SD). The degrees of freedom alone would identify what was actually computed.

questions_for_authors.question: Table II labels its dispersion 'Mean +/- SEM' (for example 51.14 +/- 9.36 at n = 22), while Tables IV and V print '+/-' with no designation in the caption, header or footnote, and the Methods define the effect size as ES = (m1 - m2)/s1 'where s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score'. Are the tabulated dispersions standard deviations or standard errors of the mean?
questions_for_authors.why: The 52 printed effect sizes and every ANOVA recomputation differ by a factor of about 4.7 between the two readings; under the SEM reading the paper's 'large' effects become small ones.

questions_for_authors.question: Three values in the Results text do not match the tables: the control group's 12-month Barthel mean is given as 59.83 in the text but 58.83 in Table II; the Group I 12-month FIM cognition score is given as 105.77 in the text but 32.73 in Table IV (105.77 being that group's total FIM score, quoted two sentences earlier); and the Group I spasticity decrement of 13.04% is not a possible share of 22 patients, where 13.64% is exactly 3 of 22 and makes the components sum to the stated 31.82%. Which value is correct in each case?
questions_for_authors.why: Three localisable discrepancies, each with an identifiable likely correction, that a corresponding author can settle from the original output in one reply.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods state that 'ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni)' was used for the between-group comparisons, but the reported values -- p = 0.040 for the SS-QOL total and p = 0.002 for the mental score, Group I versus control at 12 months -- reproduce as uncorrected two-sample tests from the Table V means and SDs (0.039 and 0.0002 pooled; 0.043 and 0.0005 Welch). Were the between-group p-values adjusted for the three group contrasts, and if so over what family?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the paper's only direct superiority claims survive the correction its own Methods describe; the SS-QOL total claim sits just inside alpha.

report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is a non-randomised, three-arm comparative study of 70 Romanian stroke patients treated at two hospitals in Baile Felix and Oradea between 2011 and 2014. One group received balneo-physiotherapy plus Lokomat robotic gait training plus intravenous Cerebrolysin (n = 22), one received balneo-physiotherapy plus Lokomat (n = 18), and one balneo-physiotherapy alone (n = 30). Patients were assessed at baseline, 6 months and 12 months on the Barthel Index, the modified Ashworth scale, the FIM and the SS-QOL. The paper concludes that combining all three therapies improves motor deficiency, spasticity, functional independence and quality of life, with the best effect sizes in the three-therapy group.

## What verified, and why that matters here

A great deal of this paper checks out, and the clean parts are what make the unclean part legible. All nine Barthel mean cells in Table II pass every granularity test applied -- 27 of 27 checks, no refusals. Across Table V's 36 SS-QOL cells, not one mean fails: 100 of 108 checks are consistent, and the eight that are not are all on the dispersion side, four of them explained by the ordinary choice of dividing by n rather than n-1. Fifty-five of 56 sums reconcile: every category count in Tables I-III sums to its group size, FIM motor plus cognition reproduces FIM total in all nine cells, SS-QOL domains reproduce the total in all nine, and the sample flow adds up. Table I's hemiplegia block looks over-subscribed until you notice it is two nested classifications, and then it reconciles cleanly. The risk-analysis paragraph is the soundest piece of work in the article: the 2x2 rebuilt from its stated proportions reproduces the reported p = 0.006 under Fisher's exact test, and both the risk ratio and the odds ratio sit at their interval midpoints on the log scale with recovered p-values bracketing it. Across 1,728 cross-group comparisons of summary statistics, no identical mean/SD pair appears.

So this is not a paper where everything is broken. The problems are two, and both are sharply localised.

## The shape of the Table IV problem

Ten of Table IV's 27 FIM means cannot be produced by any set of whole-number scores from the group sizes the table itself prints. That verdict now rests on two independent implementations: our own engine returned impossible on 18 of 18 checks for the n = 30 block when re-run in this stage, and R's `scrutiny` package independently returned inconsistent for 59.23 at n = 18 and for 88.28 and 100.85 at n = 30. Extraction error, which the base rates say should be the first suspect, is about as thoroughly excluded as it can be: the sweep reconciled Table IV against the PDF of record cell by cell, this stage re-pulled the table, and every one of the ten values is printed a second time in the Results prose. A number that appears identically in two places in the published article is not an artefact of our reading it.

The distribution of the failures is the part worth putting to the authors. All ten sit in the two comparison groups. The Cerebrolysin group's nine FIM means are all reachable -- and reachable is a narrower condition at n = 22 than at n = 30, so the asymmetry is not an artefact of group size. I draw no conclusion from this; I note that the group whose superiority the paper concludes for is the group whose numbers survive the test, and that the modal innocent explanation -- missing data shrinking the true denominator below the printed n -- is one the authors can confirm or exclude in a sentence.

## The ANOVA problem reaches further

Eight F statistics were recomputed from the paper's own printed means and standard deviations; all eight fall outside the interval those inputs permit, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of zero. This is the finding with the widest reach, because it touches all four outcomes rather than one table. What makes it resistant to a benign reading is the direction: most reported values are too small, but the SS-QOL total is too large (21.217 against an achievable 18.12 to 18.16). A repeated-measures analysis -- which is what the design actually called for, since these are three measurements on the same patients -- would raise F systematically. Reading the dispersions as the SEM that Table II's row label states would lower F drastically. Neither covers both directions, and no combination of them does.

That SD-versus-SEM ambiguity is not a pedantic point. The paper's own effect-size formula divides by "the standard deviation value of initial score", the printed effect sizes are reproduced by dividing by the tabulated dispersion, and yet Table II calls that dispersion an SEM while Tables IV and V label it as nothing at all. Mislabelling is overwhelmingly the likeliest explanation -- Olsen found 40% of studies reporting "SD" had reported the standard error, and the reverse confusion is just as ordinary -- but the reader cannot tell, and all 52 effect sizes in the paper hinge on it.

## Reporting context

None of the following makes a number wrong, but together they bear on how much external checking this work received: allocation was explicitly non-random and the paper nonetheless states flatly that no baseline characteristic differed, when the sex split alone gives p = 0.0145; there is no trial registration, no CONSORT flow diagram, and no adverse-event reporting for a protocol delivering 120 days of intravenous Cerebrolysin per patient over a year; the study is declared to have received no external funding; and a clinical stroke-rehabilitation trial containing no environmental content appears in an environmental-science journal.

## Verdict

Ten reported averages in the functional-independence table cannot have come from the samples described, confirmed by two independent engines on values printed twice in the article; and not one of the eight test statistics recomputed from the paper's own tables can be reproduced. Those numbers are the paper's evidence for one of the four outcomes in its title and for all 24 of its significance tests. I do not think the reported results can be relied upon without the raw data being made available for reanalysis.
